PRIVILEGE-MR. COLDWELL REFUSAL OF ACCESS TO PARLIAMENT BUILDINGS BY CITIZENS SEEKING TO INTERVIEW MEMBERS
speechtext:
The hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) rose yesterday afternoon at three o'clock to refer to a matter affecting the privileges of parliament and of himself as a member of parliament. I informed the hon. member that I would confer with the Clerk of the house and the Sergeant-at-Arms and that I would give him an answer as soon as possible. I have received the following memorandum from the Clerk of the House of Commons:
With regard to the admission of labour delegates and other persons in the parliament building yesterday, I have inquired from the R.C.M.P. and the house's protective staff and I have the honour to report as follows:
As we expected a large crowd yesterday and only had four constables on duty, I asked Commissioner Wood to send in a few men to help our protective staff. It is well known that the R.C.M.P. is assigned to parliament hill but the interior of the building is under the control of the protective staffs of the Senate and House of Commons.
About eleven o'clock a.m. Messrs. Murdock and Morrow, representing the delegates, called at my office and asked if they could hold a meeting in the railway committee room. I explained to

Privilege-Mr. Coldwell
them that if a member of the house desired to meet them in any committee room 1 would instruct the Sergeant-at-Arms to make the necessary preparations for the meeting to be held. They said they desired to see certain members and 1 directed them to the main entrance where they would be helped to see these members. They did this and Constables Groulx and Gauthier, not acting as policemen but in the capacity of guides, went with them and four other delegates, including a lady, to Mr. Coldwell's room. The men left them in Mr. Coldwell's secretary's office and returned to the main entrance. Some of the other delegates who had remained downstairs insisted on seeing the leaders of the C.C.F. party but were told that the party was in caucus, and our staff never interfered with such meetings. Two delegates asked that their names be sent in to Mr. Maclnnis, which was immediately granted, and the hon. member for Vancouver East came out and saw them.
Hon. Mr. Douglas, Prime Minister of Saskatchewan, told me last night that he was not prevented from coming inside the building. When he arrived at the entrance he was asked who he was and after he had given his name he was immediately allowed to go in.
I am informed by the Commissioner of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that, according to "reports he has received, none of his men stopped anybody from going inside the building.
As to the protective staff of the House of Commons, it had not been given any order by me or the Sergeant-at-Arms to keep anybody out of the building. There was some confusion when the crowd pushed in and dispersed all over the main corridor. In order to slow up this rush, the outside doors yvere closed, but not locked, for about half an hour.
It has been said in the press that "parliamentary police bar delegates from the house until members of parliament guaranteed their conduct inside." No such practice has ever existed in the parliament building. The reason why members have to be asked if they wan to see visitors is that they cannot be importuned when attending to their correspondence or other parliamentary duties. If they cannot be seen, the visitor may withdraw or sit in the corridor and wait until there is a sufficient number of visitors to be taken through the building by a guide.
You will realize, Mr. Speaker, that some precaution has to be taken in the parliament building, but our practice in this regard is very broad. The best evidence that no severity was shown yesterday is that apart from the three hundred delegates, six hundred and twenty-two other persons visited the building in addition to the five hundred who followed the debates from the galleries.
Arthur Beauchesne,
Clerk of the House of Commons.

maintopic: PROCEDURE IN QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
I would like to draw the attention of hon. members to paragraph 297, page 121 of Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition.
A certain number of oral questions are permitted in practice by members, without notice, before the orders of the day are called; but these are merely allowed by courtesy in connection "with the business of the house or with very urgent and important matters of public concern. They are always brief, no debate being permitted, and the replies are as concise as possible. The minister interrogated may-reply at once or may direct that the usual notice be given (B. 315). Such questions are governed by the same rules of order as questions of which notice has been given. (M. 245, n.4.)
Hon. members will notice that the rules say that questions are allowed by courtesy in connection with the business of the house, or with very urgent and important matters of public concern. I would like to call for the cooperation of every member and ask them not to put oral questions when they are not very urgent. It would be preferable for the dispatch of business that questions be placed on the order paper.

maintopic: PROCEDURE IN QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
PROCEDURE IN QUESTIONS ON THE ORDERS OF THE DAY
speechtext:
Before the orders of the day are called I wish to draw the attention of hon. members to a practice in debate which

is contrary to the rules of the house. I refer to the reading of speeches. Standing order No. 41 provides for decorum in debate. I would refer hon. members to Beauchesne's Parliamentary Rules and Forms, third edition, page 102, paragraphs 238 and 239, which states:
Besides the prohibition contained in this standing order, it has been sanctioned by usage both in England and in Canada, that a member, while speaking must not (a) read from a written previously prepared speech.
This rule was adopted in 1927, but as long ago as April 19, 1886, a resolution was adopted by the house which I should like to read. It was as follows:
That the growing practice in the Canadian House of Commons of delivering speeches of great length, having the character of carefully and elaborately prepared written essays, and indulging in voluminous and often irrelevant extracts, is destructive of legitimate and pertinent debate upon public questions, is a waste of valuable time, unreasonably lengthens the sessions of parliament, threatens by increased bulk and cost to lead to the abolition of the official report of the debates, encourages a discursive and diffuse, rather than an incisive and concise style of public speaking, is a marked contrast to the practice in regard to debate that prevails in the British House of Commons, and tends to repel the public from a careful and intelligent consideration of the proceedings of parliament.
No doubt it is very comforting that the written word should be before a speaker while he is addressing the house, more especially in the case of a new member, and there are many new members in the house. However, it is my duty to call the attention of hon. members of the house to the practice of reading speeches. I believe a reference to the rule in this formal and general manner will forestall any objections from the house or from the Chair in the coming debates.

The general picture is something like this. The amount covered by the war appropriation measure last year was $3,650,000,000, and the amount provided for Mutual Aid was $800,000,000, making a total of $4,450,000,000. Those are the amounts which were voted for the fiscal year 1944-45. Then for the fiscal year 1945-46 we have already voted two billion dollars. This was done at the last session.
It is estimated that an additional sum of $1,365 million will be required to meet the same class of expenditures as were covered by the votes totalling $4,450 million for the fiscal year 1944-45. There will be no Mutual Aid appropriation at this session of parliament. None will be proposed by the government. The two billions of dollars voted at the last session could be used either for ordinary war purposes or for Mutual Aid. Mutual Aid has ended, and it will not be necessary for us to have any further Mutual Aid appropriation. So that the amount of $1,365 million which is covered by the second resolution found on the order paper under government notices of motions will be for ordinary, war and demobilization purposes. I think it can be said that the expenditures are those necessarily made as a result of the war.
When the resolution and bill voting $1,365 million come before the house opportunities for debate will be given, as they have been in the past. To-day I am asking the house for only $400 million.

As you know, Mr. Chairman, there is an insistent demand all over the country that the government should make some declaration of policy regarding control bodies and bureaucratic expenditures which are being made over the head of parliament by certain bodies which have been set up. I will refer to this matter for only two or three minutes. For years past we have been told, by Mr. Churchill in the British House of Commons, an)d more or less by our own Prime Minister here, I believe, that once the war ceased these controls and other war expenditures would cease and we would regain what we, the high court of parliament, surrendered when the war broke out, namely control of expenditures. At the present time we have virtually no control. All kinds of bodies, over the head of parliament, are spending money like water. Every principle for which the British nation struggled in the old 'land since the seventeenth century has been surrendered -to the political caucuses. Parliament itself, which came into being to ensure that taxes shall be voted only by those who have to pay them, has become the institution through which those who do not pay them impose them on others.
I want to emphasize to the committee that powers of legislation older even than the right
of taxpayers to determine the national expenditure have been surrendered, and if we are to continue this sort of thing the power of parliament will be gone forever. Whole spheres of activity, involving the livelihood of every man, woman and child in this country, have been removed from the jurisdiction of the law and of parliament and reserved for the determination of tribunals, irresponsible, irremovable, governed by no control and subject to no appeal. I do object, now that the war is over, to the way that business is being conducted over the head of parliament. We are told that parliament is supreme. That is only a myth. If parliament is supreme, why has it not now control over these outside bodies and their expenditures and in the result we will only hold a post mortem as the money is spent.
I come from a very large taxpaying city. The working class have to pay a twelve per cent sales tax and the burden of taxation is very heavy upon them and upon business firms in the district. Some small business men have been put out of business altogether. As I go along the streets in the large city from which I come I get numerous complaints as to the way these war-time organizations have been carrying on. I protest against the continuation of these irksome controls. I wish to assert the supremacy of parliament over these outside bodies. A large number of them have not contributed a snap of the fingers to the winning of the war, yet they continue to spend hundreds of millions of dollars. As one goes around the country one sees how the money is being wasted. There is no retrenchment, no economy, no peace yet. We do not know even that the war is over yet. We did not know, thanks to our new status, that the war had started until ten days after it did, but the Canadians who were on board the Athenia on September 5, 1939, when it was sunk, found out that Canada was at war.
One might as well drop the theory that parliament is supreme. We are not supreme, or we would have control. What I should like to see is a reform of parliament whereby members of all groups would get together and decide what is best to be done for the taxpayers. We have put up with the present conditions in war time for long enough, dear knows.

Mr. Speaker, following the
example given by those who spoke in this debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, I promise to confine myself to a few very brief remarks. First, Mr. Speaker, I wish to tender you my congratulations, which you deserve because we are all sure that, with your deep understanding of men and things, with your parliamentary experience, it will be easy for you to preserve the traditions of dignity and impartiality which the House of Commons has known under your predecessors. The honour which has been conferred on you, is reflected on your compatriots and on the province which you represent. I am sure that Canada as a whole, and more especially the province of Quebec, is grateful to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and to the house for having selected you as Speaker.
May I also compliment the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. While new'comers in this house, our two fellow-members have shown a self-assurance and a judgment which do them honour and bode well for their political career which I hope will be long and fruitful both for themselves and for the electors who have made such a happy choice in sending them to this house as the representatives of the fine constituencies of Kenora-Rainy River and Gaspe. Incidentally, I also congratulate our colleague from Gaspe on having won his election, thereby adding one more constituency to those held by the Liberal party.
On June 11 last, the Canadian people gave a clear, unequivocal and definite verdict whereby the hon. members of this house were given a clear-cut mandate. That victory of the Liberal party led by the Right Hon. William Lyon Mackenzie King, was won in this country through the prestige of its leader and also because of the quality of the policies he advocates. Congratulations must be directed to our political leader for the manner in which he conducted that election which put the Liberal party again in power. It is mainly
[Mr. Abbott. 1
because of his administration of the last ten years that the Right Hon. the Prime Minister was able to achieve that victory. His administration, especially since we entered war alongside the United Nations, has placed our country, from an international as well as a national standpoint in the rank it deserves. His attendance, and that of the hon. Minister of Justice (Mr. St. Laurent) at the San Francisco conference, the presence of Canadian delegates at the Bretton Woods conference, and other events in the international field, have put our country in a position such that we can to-day claim that it is one of the great powers of the world and that it can, because of the sacrifices of its children, claim the privileges of an autonomous and free nation among the free countries of the world.
The San Francisco conference, especially, has commanded the attention of the Canadian people because the delegates who represented us there accomplished splendid work. By way of digression, may I be permitted to thank, in behalf of myself and my electors, the Right Hon. the Prime Minister of Canada and his distinguished colleague from the province of Quebec, the honourable Minister of Justice, for having caused the French language to be recognized as official in the discussions of the San Francisco conference. One thing which must also be emphasized is the stand they took at that time when they defended vigorously and successfully the rights of minor nations. Small nations, Mr. Speaker, are not unlike small men. They are sometimes overwhelmed by the physical stature of those who surround them. Thanks to the intervention of Canada's representatives at the San Francisco conference, the preponderant voices of small nations have been recognized and today our country and others of equal rank are empowered to claim their rights in such conferences.
The administration of the Prime Minister, in sending ambassadors to certain countries of the world, has done something which had the direct consequence of making felt in the whole world the influence and the genius of Canada. On this account, Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister and his government deserve conmenda-tion.
In some quarters the present government is charged with not giving our country all the attention it deserves in the field of international emancipation. iMr. Speaker, Canada is gradually being emancipated thanks to our government's policy, although, as far as I can see, the Quebec nationalist publications have refrained from congratulating those who are courageously bringing about the change; true, these men do not'seek the limelight, but they

The Address-Mr. Lalonde
work with an effectiveness which remains unparalleled by any government since the days of confederation.
Mr. Speaker, in the national sphere, as is indicated in the throne speech, our government has promoted peace and order, it has profoundly stimulated our national life, which achievement deserves recognition. Indeed, recent events may have surprised some people, and in order to be understood by my Englishspeaking colleagues, may I say this to them:
(Text): Certain sections of the Canadian electorate were quite surprised at the way the province of Quebec voted in the federal election on June 11 last. Many of our compatriots in the western provinces, and I may add in the central and maritime provinces as well, really felt that we would embrace extreme nationalism. This was the argument used against us on the hustings and in the newspapers of our opponents throughout the whole dominion. Such extremists as Reverend Mr. Shields even invoked the spectre of Roman domination by Quebec over the rest of Canada. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, the whole province of Quebec remained faithful to its traditions of order and peace. It voted for the Liberal party because this party, more than any other, offered what I might call the ideal of social and moral security, by applying merely the formula of common sense. In spite of what our good friends opposite may think, the province of Quebec has remained the fortress of political traditions because in those traditions, strengthened by the teachings of the past, are to be found the elements of political economy and social stability. We did not pay heed to calls of integral Toryism, which we believed inspired by doubtful political aims. We discarded the spectre of socialism of the C.C.F. party, whose theories cannot be adapted to the demands of our scholastic doctrines-and I say that in all sincerity to my hon. friends opposite. We remained firmly set in the Canadian federation. We understood the true and only vocation of the French-Canadian people who obeyed the act of Providence, understood and realized that the future of this country is always directly dependent upon the maintenance of the confederation link under the protection of a revived constitution. And all those who believed that we wanted political revolution in order to foster the shameful ambitions of separatism did not understand and have not understood the real and true mentality of my compatriots from Quebec.
We never asked for arbitrary privileges. We are convinced that no progress is possible for 47696-6J
Canada without the sincere cooperation of all the racial elements which make up the Canadian nation. National salvation cannot be attained by imposing excessive and humiliating formulae or by taking arrogant and rigid attitudes. Brutal realism teaches us that our problems can always be solved if we tackle them with a broad understanding of the legitimate aspirations of the sections concerned.
Exelusivism and fanaticism have never produced progressive measures either for the oppressed minorities or for the majorities abusing their rights or their strength. A sincere mutual understanding is the source of all honourable agreements. The unjust demands of a majority, and the violent denunciations of a noisy minority, cannot create the right atmosphere necessary to the acceptance of the mutual agreements required for the progress of the nation. Peace is engendered by mutual sacrifices freely accepted. This is what my compatriots understood when once more they endorsed the King-St. Laurent government. I am convinced that they will not be deceived.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, a few weeks ago, an extremely important event took place in Ottawa. I refer to the federal-provincial conference attended by the premiers of all the provinces of the dominion. The foundations were set for a revision of the confederation pact and subjects of discussion were chosen for the next few months.
I do not intend to take up too much of your time, but I am convinced that a serious study of the preliminary discussions will convince us that the various parties are agreed on the necessity of amending the British North America Act.. I am not a sponsor of centralization and I am ready to put up an energetic fight against any useless centralization; however, all constitutional measures, as well as all positive human legislation remain, to my mind, open to evolution and progress. Indeed, by stubbornly refusing to amend the British North America Act for reasons of petty politics would constitute a negation of all progress.
It has become imperative that our constitutional instrument be amended and revised to conform to present needs. It behooves us to open our eyes and forget for a moment, if I may be allowed to say so, those people who are concerned with their exclusive interests and inspired by petty political considerations alone, to apply our minds to promoting the welfare of the community. Such a progressive object will ever remain unobtainable in our country if we rely on a constitutional pact which is obsolete and has become inadequate to solve the problems which face us to-day.
The Address-Mr. Lalonde

Some of our opponents claim that the fact of amending the constitutional act would constitute an infringement of racial and religious rights. Members of the Bloc Populaire are present in this house and I would say to them that the real defenders of constitution in parliament were never the Quebec nationalists but rather the representatives of the government presently in power who have succeeded in safeguarding the rights of my race and religion in the province of Quebec.
Arguments to the effect that our province has been denied the constitutional privileges it enjoys have been too often expounded in this house and outside of it. I trust that, under the wise guidance of the present federal government, if an amendment to our constitution be enacted, the interests of minorities and dissident groups will be fully safeguarded.
Mr. Speaker, now that the war is ended, we must turn our attention to the economic and social reconstruction of our country. Tremendous sums have been spent to eradicate evil and to bring truth out of chaos. I do not regret the tragic lessons of history or the tragic teachings of the war which has just ended, but I am convinced that the events of recent years have opened widely the eyes of some of the extremists of my province and that they shall accept henceforth the brutal reality of the responsibilities which lie upon the shoulders of a self-respecting nation.
(Text).: The awful nightmare of war has disappeared. We are entering an eTa of peaceful reconstruction. Our mandate strictly compels us to forget our political differences in order to think only of Canada's interests. I do not doubt that every hon. member shares my view in this matter. We therefore turn our eyes toward the horizon of peace. The task is immense and difficult. To direct Canada toward its final destiny in a world that is still labouring under wounds left by the war and to maintain it in its proper rank among the union of free nations will be the noble and magnificent work of this Canadian parliament, and all the members of the house.
We will set our whole heart and all our strength upon this task, Mr. Speaker, during the years to come. We will work without respite in order that all our compatriots, from the highest rank to the humblest labourer, can assert, when we appear before the tribunal of public opinion, "This man has deserved well of his country".

Mr. Speaker, I trust it will not be considered presumption on the part of one who has been in this house for so short a time to rise thus 
early in the debate on the speech from the throne; but I do so because of my intense interest in the welfare of those old comrades of mine who served in this war and in the first world war-an interest which I believe is shared by all hon. members.
I know that you will realize that a new member standing on his feet for the first time in the House of Commons is under considerable strain. I remember the great men who have sat in these seats before me for many years, and I hope that their wisdom, their courage and their ability will nerve me to do the task which I see before me, to-day and in the months to come.
I represent, sir, the most westerly of all constituencies, that of Nanaimo, on the southern portion of Vancouver island. It is a paradise, but I would not like anybody to feel that it is by any means an old man's home, because there are great industries in that constituency, and great natural resources to be developed which will give employment for our returning service men.
Amongst those industries I would like to refer for a moment to the logging industry. We have a climate which combines bright sunshine and a good deal of moisture; this enables trees to grow to immense height and great girth. That logging industry has been an essential industry during these war years, and will be during the years of reconstruction. It is on the very threshhold of great and new developments, such as the production of plywoods and plastics and the utilization of the various waste products of the forest. Conditions in the camps are infinitely better than they were a few years ago, and they offer to returning men a clean, wholesome and out-of-door life which I am sure will be attractive to a great many of our soldiers, sailors and airmen. New machinery has been introduced. The industry needs outside help, because the men connected with it have been struggling during these war years. The actual loggers, the employees, the members of the I.W.A., have adhered most rigidly during all these years to their nonstrike pledge. The operational branches of the industry have not always been able to select the best timber from their point of view for cutting, but have answered nobly to the request of the government to turn out every foot of lumber that they possibly could. The companies and the loggers themselves have paid large amounts into the dominion treasury by virtue of their income taxes and excess profit returns. Might I suggest that, in order to sustain the yield, the government might see fit to encourage

The Address-Mr. Pearkes
that industry and to help in some measure to remove or lessen the danger of the great bugbear of the logging industry, which is the forest fire. If we can have a sustained yield we can give employment to many returned men.
Another industry I should like to mention is that of our commercial and sporting fisheries. The harvest of our ocean consists of many varieties of fish-salmon, cod, halibut, tuna, pilchards; even the dogfish, for the sake of its liver; the oyster; also the seaweed-all opening up grand opportunities for returning men to follow that particular kind of work. Never before have the fishermen of British Columbia had such fine floating equipment as they have to-day. Science has come to the help of the fisherman by giving him means of locating shoals of fish, of improving the system of transporting to the markets the fish which have been caught, and of presenting them in better condition than ever before.
These fishermen do not congregate and live in the big cities; they prefer to have their families scattered among a number of small towns throughout Vancouver island. But while their floating equipment is better now than ever before, they need protection during the winter storms for that floating equipment. Before the war that industry was largely in the hands of the Japanese, and the Japanese drove many of our white fishermen off our Canadian waters. The money they made they sent back to a foreign land. To-day our white fishermen have captured that trade and are spending their money in Canada. Never again must Japanese be allowed to capture the fishing industry of British Columbia.
I have not time this afternoon to go into any great detail regarding the mining industry and the agriculture of British Columbia. I would like to say one word about the great number of people who cater to the visitors who come to our island. They are in all kinds of little private enterprises, such as the corner grocery store, the wayside garage, the hotel, the tourist camp. Those people have been struggling during this war because, due to restrictions on gasoline and difficulties of transportation, the number of visitors has not been as great as in pre-war days. The younger men from those families have in the main joined the armed services and gone overseas. Their parents have shown commendable courage in keeping homes together during these years and in struggling to earn their livelihood. Their great hopes are that their sons and daughters will soon return from the duties they have undertaken in the defence of their country, and that the burden of
taxation will be relieved so as to enable them to establish gainful business for those sons and daughters when they return.
When V-E Day was declared in Europe it was announced that the Canadian army would be required to provide an occupational force for Germany, also a Far Eastern Force for war against Japan, and that surplus personnel would be' returned to their homes as soon as they could be spared, it being recognized that some would have to remain on in essential positions. The men who volunteered for the Far Eastern Force and for the occupational army were in the main younger men who had not seen quite so much service, had not been subjected to the toils and brunt of battle quite so much as those who had gone overseas either with the 1st or 2nd Canadian division in 1939 and 1940.
It was announced that the surplus which very largely consisted of those men who had borne the brunt of battle for the longest time, would be returned upon a point system, and the points were announced as being two points for every month of service in Canada, three points for every month of service in a theatre of war, and a bonus if a man was married. It was generally believed that the policy of first-in, first-out, would be followed as closely as it was practical for the authorities to adhere to that policy. Everybody realized that it was not possible to adhere rigidly to the first-in, first-out policy but that exceptions would have to be made of some key personnel who would have to be retained overseas, as well as releasing some to industry and other walks of life, of men for higher education, special training and so forth. But the country believed, and the constituents of Nanaimo believed, that so far as possible, the-policy would be adhered to of returning first those men who had served the longest so>
that they might have the first opportunity of becoming reestablished and fitting themselves into civilian life.
Gradually that policy has been whittled down, and I have prepared a list of exceptions which have been made which I should like to give to the house because I think it will show to hon. members that that policy has been departed from far more than the people of this country ever expected it would be.
This is the list of exceptions. First of all, all men who were on compassionate leave on V-E day, provided they were on compassionate leave on V-J day, would be granted their discharge. This and the following exceptions all apply to the army in Canada. So far as the army overseas was concerned we were told that the men were to be brought back on a
The Address-Mr. Pearkes

point-score system, and as an example of how they would be brought back, the official pamphlet gave these figures:
If 20,000 were to be sent back during one of the early months of demobilization, 5,000 would have a point-score of between 225 and 250, 5,000 between 200 and 225, and 10,000 between 175 and 200. I want hon. members to notice the points which an overseas man was required to have in order to expect early demobilization.
To come back to the list, those men of the army in Canada who were on compassionate leave on V-E day, provided they were on compassionate leave on V-J day, may be discharged. The same thing applies to those who were on compassionate farm leave, and to men who desired to go to college or university provided they had a written acceptance from the university officials. They also may be discharged. Men on account of what may be considered their age or low pulhem profile, even though that pulhem profile is not so low as to render them physically unfit, and for whom no employment could be found in the army, may be discharged. Any man who on March 31 of this year had a point-score of 130 may be discharged if he is in Canada. Any man who is returned wounded, any repatriated prisoner of war; any man *who served during the war of 1914-18; any *man who has reached the age of forty-two; [DOT]any man, no matter how short a time he has served in the army in Canada, provided he 'held a job at the time of his enlistment, -no matter for how short a time, if only for one day, may be discharged if he has a score *of 105 points. If he has not 105 points, he may receive long-term leave so that he may, I presume, get thoroughly reestablished in that job before a man with a higher point-score comes back from overseas. Any lad who had not reached his nineteenth birthday; young men, who I suggest might well benefit by a few months in the Canadian army where they could relieve a long-term service man; any man who is still retained at the district depot and has not been passed on to the training camp established at Vernon; any man who can claim to be going to employment of national importance-any man who is illiterate; any man who is unable to speak English or French sufficiently to receive training-all these may be discharged. This Mr. Speaker, is throwing the gates wide open. A soldier may go up to the sergeant-major, and if he cannot speak French, all he has to do is to shrug his shoulders and say, "Me no speak English" and he is out-out to go and seek a job before the long-service men come back from overseas.

Any man who is considered by his commanding officer as untrainable because he may be considered unreliable, and any man can pose as being unreliable; any man who is indifferent to service; in other words, any man who does not want to be a soldier, any man who will not respond to discipline-these are the men that you are letting out to go and seek jobs which the men who have been bearing the brunt of this war cannot come back and seek.
I realize that shipping is a difficulty and they cannot come back all at once. But why is any man who is serving in Canada now able to go out and take the jobs which are now available and which are growing fewer and fewer as the weeks and months go by?
It is for these reasons that I charge that the government is demobilizing our service forces to the detriment of the men who have fought the longest. Thirty or forty years ago Mr. Rudyard Kipling wrote a poem which I quote in part:
A man o' four-an'-twenty that 'asn't learned of a trade-
Beside "Reserve" agin' his name-'e'd better never been made.
These men who are overseas went over four or five years ago at the age of nineteen, twenty or twenty-one. They have reached their twenty-fourth birthday and they will find it increasingly difficult to find jobs in which they may learn a trade. Perhaps it is because of that that last week it was announced in the papers that there was to be a continuing army in Canada, a continuing army because of the uncertain condition in the world, because we could not foresee what dangers might arise. Nobody will take exception to that. Service in that continuing army was however restricted to those men who are in the active army or who have recently left the active army and would like to come back again. But there was one condition set, namely, that they must be prepared to serve wherever Canada required them to serve-a reasonable condition. At the same time we are continuing another or second continuing army, a continuing army of fine young men of good physique who have had months of training and who are not eligible for the first continuing army because they are not prepared to go and serve wherever Canada wants them to serve should an emergency arise.
[Mr. Pearkes. 1

The Address-Mr. Zaplitny
I have not the up-to-date figures, but the last figures which were published showed that there were some 16,000 of these N.R.M.A. soldiers still in Canada who were fit for the infantry and some twelve or fourteen thousand who were fit for the other arms of the service. Some of these men will desire to get out of the army, but there are a great many of them who like the security of the Canadian army in Canada. They are provided with three meals a day. They have comfortable lodgings in hutments. They have hot and cold water laid on. They have officers who will endeavour to make their training as interesting as possible. They are provided with free picture shows and all types of recreation. Only two weeks ago a sports meeting was held in Victoria where men of this type were brought in at the country's expense from all over British Columbia in order that they might show their physical prowess.
These men like to serve in the Canadian army provided they are not ordered to go wherever Canada may require them. You may say that if an emergency comes they will then be ordered to go. If an emergency comes it may come quickly and we shall want trained men. But an army is not made up purely and solely of trained men. It is made up of trained units which have been welded together; and I tell you, speaking as an old soldier, that the veteran and the shirker wifi not work in harness together during that period of training in Canada. Therefore efficiency is lost, and all the time additional taxation is required in order to maintain this second continuing army.
The Secretary of State yesterday referred in glowing terms to the contributions Canada had made to this war. We were all proud to hear of that effort. But, sir, I claim that there is one blot on that escutcheon and it is now time to remove it. We should no longer have this bifocal army through which one class of men see it as their duty to go wherever their country calls them while the other class see their duty as lying only in so far as the shores of Canada restrict their activities.
I said that we have in Nanaimo opportunities for absorbing the men who come back from overseas in the reconstruction and in the development of our industries and national resources. I said that the people of my constituency urgently require their boys back from overseas. They desire relief from taxation. It is because, as I have shown to-day, the demobilization as now being carried out is working to the serious disadvantage of our men overseas that I support the amendment which has been put forward by our leader, and I
believe that every returned man in this house, irrespective of the party to which he belongs, should support that amendment for that reason. Furthermore, I believe that the maintenance, the continuation of this futile two-army system should cease immediately.
