On the very eve of the
meeting of this parliament the government announced by order in council it had effected some amendments to the National Housing Act. With the text of those amendments I do not propose to deal this evening. They may be good or they may be bad; I do not make any comment in that respect. But I do say that the house is entitled to a clear explanation as to why amendments were so urgently required to a statute which had been in effect and on the statute books for fifteen months that they could not wait and be presented in parliament, and that they had to be dealt with at an earlier date.
Another example which surprised some of us was the government's action in connection with hauling down the union jack the day parliament met. We are told in the speech

from the throne that we are to have a committee to go into the question of a design of a distinctive flag for this country. At the moment I am not discussing the question of a distinctive flag. I am saying that the action of the government in hauling down one flag and putting up another, while going through the form of saying that parliament will deal with the matter was high-handed. If they can pull down one flag and put up another, they can pull down the second flag and put up a third and so on. When is this to stop? I say it was a high-handed action, and coming as it did on the day parliament opened it amounted to a flouting of parliament.
There are some lessons which can well be drawn from experience of recent days- yes, from the election itself. Even though my leader is not Prime Minister of this country to-day as I had hoped and expected he would be, I am proud to be his follower. He fought a good fight for a worthy cause and there was nothing he said or did of which he has any cause to be ashamed. I am proud to follow him. I believe that the time will come when our good compatriots in the province of Quebec will come to know John Bracken and will appreciate his sincerity, his honesty of purpose, and will accord to him their support.
During the course of the debate we have heard some suggestions-perhaps they are more than suggestions-that the party which sits to your right, Mr. Speaker, has the unqualified support of organized labour throughout the Dominion of Canada. In the light of the facts such a suggestion creates a certain amount of amusement. In the first place we are told about the Prime Minister's profound sympathy for labour and about his profound knowledge of the problems of labour.
I suggest that it is worth remembering that when a dominion-provincial conference was called in the fall of 1943 to evolve a national labour code which would assure to labour in all parts of the country its right of collective bargaining, unfortunately that profound sympathy did not grasp the opportunity to put into effect a labour code which would apply to all industry throughout Canada. Eight provinces out of the nine asked the dominion to do it; but because one province said "no", the government, notwithstanding its alleged profound sympathy for labour, said, "We will just confine it to war industry". A great opportunity was lost. I hope a similar opportunity will present itself, but I repeat that a great opportunity was lost and an injustice done to labour. I think it is worth while recalling also what happened on parliament hill yesterday. If there are those on

The Address-Mr. Fleming
the other side of the house who feel secure in the support of organized labour, I suggest to them that in my humble opinion it is a good thing for them that the election is past and that they are not facing it again.
We have been told from the government side of the house about the partnership which the government entered into during war time with labour and industry. That may be the government's idea, but it certainly is not the idea of organized labour. Organized labour feels that its offer of cooperation with the government in meeting problems which could be met only by the united action of government, labour and industry in war time was not accepted by the government or used as it might have been.
There is one further observation I should like to make about something that we have read in the papers of recent date. I refer to the reported remarks of the leader of the C.C.F. group (Mr. Coldwell) in the newspapers of last week. He is reported to have intimated that the party which he leads will be the only real opposition to the government in this house. It must have been a very dull evening that required such an extraordinary pleasantry from the leader of that group in order to enliven the hours. If anyone has any doubt about the position of those of us who stand under the Progressive Conservative banner with respect to opposition to government policy and government action they will find an effective answer in the statesmanlike utterances delivered by our leader yesterday afternoon.
Political memory may be short but it is well to remember what happened in Ontario between June 4 and June 11. There are some hon. members opposite who well remember what happened between those dates. There was a shift of support by many thousands of C.C.F. voters to government candidates. In other words, there are at least a dozen members on the other side of this house who owe their seats in this chamber to C.C.F. support which swung the tide in their favour. When we are asked to consider some other group as being the real effective opposition to this government it is well to remember that those twelve seats are essential to the continuance of this government in office. We should not forget where that support came from on that occasion.
It is well also to remember some of the events of last November. It will not be forgotten that in the momentous days in this house in November last it remained for the C.C.F. group to agree sufficiently with the government in connection with meeting the needs of man-power to unite with them by
passing an effective amendment which called forth an expression of appreciation on the part of the Prime Minister. I do not think there is any doubt as to where the real opposition is to be found. The answer is that the real opposition lies right here, and it will be a constructive opposition.
The decade of the thirties surely taught Canada some lessons. One lesson which we ought to have learned is that if we are to avoid great industrial and economic dislocations we must make ample preparation in advance. There is no use in waiting until these great dislocations are upon us to begin to plan measures to cope with them. I have sat in this chamber for only four days and I have followed the proceedings with no little interest. Perhaps the impressions of a newcomer to this chamber are fresh and vivid, but one impression that has been borne upon my mind is the amazing vagueness of the statements emanating from the government with reference to the whole problem of reconversion.
The leader of the opposition made some direct criticisms in his remarks yesterday, and I fully expected that we would have from the Prime Minister or other members of the government-at least one other member has spoken-some clear exposition in concrete form of the programme offered by the government to meet this great national emergency which is upon us. But instead of that we have had only vague and general statements; there has been nothing concrete.
Obviously the government has been taken unawares; obviously the government has been caught unprepared. The Secretary of State (Mr. Martin) is reported in the press as having said in Port Hope on September 3 that the government had not been in a position to foresee that the atomic bomb would have brought the war to such a speedy conclusion and that its plans for economic postwar stabilization would have been more effective had there been more time to put them into effect. Then we have the Premier of Manitoba speaking in the legislature of that province and being reported as saying on September 4:
Premier Garson told the legislature, sitting as a committee of the whole on post-war plans, that all-important negotiations between the dominion government and the provinces were many months away from conclusion. "Instead of just now starting negotiations, we should be in a position to start work," he said.
The only suggestion I have heard from any member' of the government that they have a programme for this period of reconversion was a reference to the dominion-provincial conference and the proposals there made to the
The Address-Mr. Fleming

governments of the provinces. That was a conference held in Ottawa in August last, and it will convene again in December. Apparently we are asked to infer that action on the part of the government must await decisions emanating from that conference. If in the view of the government action must await the conclusion of that conference, why on earth, Mr. Speaker, was that conference not called long ago? There was no reason given to the conference for the delay that has occurred in calling it together. The government of Ontario, from the time it came into office in August, 1943, begged and clamoured for a dominion-provincial conference with this very objective in mind, that the governments of all the provinces and the government of the dominion might sit down together and plan jointly so that this period of conversion might be bridged without loss of employment and without complete dislocation. That request went begging. For two years the provinces have waited, and when finally they were brought together it was on the eve of the conclusion of hostilities with Japan. If the government's plans are dependent on the conclusion of the negotiations with the provincial governments, then this government stands condemned for its long delay, a delay of at least two years, in summoning that essential conference. They should have had their plans complete long ago. They knew that the war was going to end some time and that it would be too late then to start planning. Why not at least get plans well under way beforehand, so that when the war did end, regardless of whether is was sooner or later, the plans would be ready and work could proceed?
There is no problem before this house that is more urgent than the problem of housing. It has two aspects which cannot be dissociated from one another-the emergency aspect, and the long-term approach to the problem.
In the first place it is admitted on all sides that an acute housing emergency exists, the worst of its kind in the history of the country. There never has been a time when Canada faced a housing problem nearly as acute as the present one. It is worth examining into the causes of the problem.
What are the causes? Sad to say, Mr. Speaker, some chickens are coming home to roost. The reason why this country is not better provided with skilled labour and building materials essential to the construction of homes is largely attributable to the failure of the government to apply a courageous and effective man-power policy during the war. The fact that tens of thousands of men were kept in enforced idleness or at least were removed from productive enterprise and were not being used where they were required in

the country's service is directly the cause of the fact that we have this acute shortage of materials and this acute shortage of skilled labour. Lumber production was allowed to fall seriously below the figure at which it should have been maintained. Five billion feet was the production of four years ago, and that figure should and could have been maintained if an effective man-power policy had been applied by the government. Unless the discharges from active service are speeded up and men are available at once not only in the construction industry but in the primary production of the essentials of building materials it will be too late for this winter's production in the seasonal producing areas. Internal production restrictions should be removed at once, and serious consideration must be given by the government to the curtailment of our substantial export of lumber to the United States.
During all this period there has been a government agency called Wartime Housing Limited, which has 'been used by the government in certain ways. It was used by the government in wartime to 'build semi-permanent houses to house certain industrial workers and it is now being used in certain localities to build what are called permanent houses.
Of the operations of Wartime Housing Limited I say only this at the present time: If the government had given private builders the same opportunities to obtain materials and labour that Wartime Housing Limited enjoyed they could and would have done better work more quickly and at far less cost.
The methods of that government housing agency were on many occasions high-handed. We had some experience of that in Toronto. We asked them to come to the assistance of the city, where a critical problem has existed now for a long time, and when they finally consented to come in, it was on the basis of the city giving up to them its best sites. They were not satisfied with anything but the best. Their attitude was: AVartime Housing must not lose a cent. Their attitude was not: There has been a tremendous influx of workers into your city, some 75,000, and we will provide the housing that is required. No; the attitude of Wartime Housing was: AVe are not going to lose one cent on this proposition and we must have your best sites. Even the health bydaws of Toronto had to be suspended to enable AA'artime Housing Limited to go ahead. That was their high-handed and dictatorial attitude.
With this same control-complex this government agency has prevented private builders from making their most effective contribution to meeting the need for housing.
AVe cannot separate the failure of the government to act courageously in this wartime

The Address-Mr. Fleming
housing problem from its failure to bring to the -whole housing problem in Canada a sensible, comprehensive, courageous and long-term view.
This house has been told that the National Housing Act of 1944 was the government's answer to the housing problem. Let us remember in the first place that that measure is administered by the Department of Finance. Let us remember also that Wartime Housing Limited and the so-called emergency measures taken by the government in war time come under the administration of the Department of Munitions and Supply. And now we have the Department of Veterans Affairs coming into the picture and becoming involved in the housing problem. What is needed is not a few more departments involving themselves in this problem. What the situation requires is an active housing policy from this government. We can keep on adding to the departments becoming involved in the problem, but that does not give us a policy; it simply adds to the conifusion already existing. It is time that the government grappled with the problem courageously and realized once and for all that more departments and further interdepartmental competition will not build more houses for the people of Canada.
I offer these observations, Mr. Speaker. First there has been a complete inadequacy of planning on the part of this government. Just-outside Toronto at the present time Wartime Housing Limited is building, at the instance of the Department of Veterans Affairs, six hundred houses for returning veterans-six hundred houses in a city that sent overseas tens of thousands of men who are now coming back! That apparently is the answer of the government to the housing problem in that great-city. My leader yesterday used the expression "too little and too late" as applied to the government's action in this respect. If I may use his language I would go a ste-p further and say that the government's action is far too little and far too late.
In the next place, the government has been doing far too much talking about what it intended to do in the realm of housing, leading the people of Canada to expect great things. The fact of the matter is that, unless they have something which they have not yet shown this chamber, they cannot possibly hope to fulfil the promises they made to the people, and many thousands of people, disappointed Canadians, are going to be living under conditions of great hardship this winter because of the failure of the government to make good and fulfil its undertakings to the Canadian people.
Next, in regard to the government's approach to this problem, particularly as evidenced in the National Housing Act, I say that the approach has been financial rather than social. This housing problem is a social problem. The government has not approached it as such but has treated it simply as a financial problem, and we shall not have a sympathetic and effective approach to the housing problem in this country unless it is seen as a social and not merely as a financial problem.
Here is this National Housing Act of 1944. It is an enabling statute. Consider these terms as found, for example, in section 4: "The minister may enter into contracts"; section 6: "The minister may by agreement" do thus and so; section 7: The minister may make loans; section 8: The minister may make loans; section 9: The minister may make loans to certain institutions; section 10: The governor in council may do certain things. And so on all through the act. It is an enabling statute; and therefore the approach of the administration to that act, and the spirit in which it undertakes to carry out parliament's expectations in respect of that statute, are allimportant, and I say that on the record of the government in the fifteen months that statute has been on the statute books of the country the government has shown itself unwilling to deal with or at least indifferent to the immensity of the problem. It has not taken this statute in hand and sought to give a sympathetic application to it or to make its provisions workable and available to all Canadians.
For example, the government has refused the request of certain municipalities for permission to set up low-dividend housing corporations. In some places, for instance in Ontario, the provincial government offered to share half of the public ten per cent contribution to low rental projects, sharing that cost with the city of Toronto. That seemed a reasonable proposition, where you get a provincial government coming forward hand in hand with a great city and offering to share half the public contribution of ten per cent to a low rental housing project.
What happened? The Department of Finance, administering the statute, simply turned them down, and there has not been a zealous, sympathetic application of the provisions of this statute to meet the housing needs of the country. Far more use could be made of the provisions of this statute than has been made.
The approach that those of us on this side of the house in the Progressive Conservative party make to this housing programme can

The Address-Mr. Fleming
best be summed up in this sentence. We regard it as a social problem which must be approached along with our approach to other social problems, and in working out for Canadians a sensible and comprehensive programme of social security we say that this must have its due place. We bring to this problem certain convictions. In the first place, we say that in any of these social security measures you must first of all avoid duplication of facilities, because that only breeds waste and competition, and I for one have not yet seen the necessity for the dominion going ahead and setting up machinery to administer social measures such as family allowances, while the governments of the provinces have trained staffs fitted to handle social and welfare problems, which staffs have been sidetracked in that matter.
We are all Canadians, whether as members of parliament or of legislatures, whether as members of the federal government or members of provincial governments, and surely to goodness it ought to be possible in these social measures to find some common ground and make a non-political and constructive approach having regard to the needs of the people of Canada, instead of setting up duplication by way of competitive methods of administration. This is wasteful and it breeds chaos in matters of administration.
In the second place, we say that in matters of social security there is never any excuse for hiding costs. In my experience of some years in the city council of Toronto, where we had many housing problems, and socialists and communists from time to time sat in the council, I always observed this with the socialists and communists in their approach to housing problems as in regard to any other social problems, that they preferred not to see the cost segregated and made known. Where it came to municipal assistance to any housing projects the idea always was to cover it up in terms of some low fixed assessment or some low fixed tax. Our obligation to the people to whom we are responsible is to see that they understand what these measures cost. The people wish to know these things, and it is our duty to give them this information. Let us know what the cost is. Do not let us endeavour at any time to hide these costs under cover. Hidden subsidies have no place in any approach to housing. In advocating subsidies in certain cases let us know what they are; let us make them known.
In the third place, we ought to make sure that the benefits of projects which are undertaken by parliament are assured to those for whom they are intended and not provide

measures which admit at any time of these benefits not being passed on to those for whom they are meant. In matters of that kind as in all matters, but particularly in that respect, it is desirable that the local governments be used in connection with administration. We shall get the most efficient, the most effective, yes, and the most understanding administration of these measures if they are carried out by the local authorities who know the local situation and the local needs.
In the fourth place, all these social measures ought to be designed to help people to help themselves. That is the view of people who are experienced in social work and parliament ought to have due regard to that view. In whatever measures we undertake we ought to seek to avoid the discouragement of thrift and enterprise.
Having said that, what is our view in regard to the necessity for a comprehensive and long-range approach to the problem of housing? In the first place it must be comprehensive. There must be no piecemeal approach to the question of social security. We have suffered too long from competition between governments and between sections of the country in matters of social security. There must be a comprehensive plan rather than a piecemeal, political approach.
In the next place, having regard to the constitutional difficulties, whereas the great sources of taxation are placed within the power of parliament, the responsibility and jurisdiction with respect to social measures have been placed in the provinces. This inverted relationship must be corrected by constitutional action or agreement particularly in facing up to the problem of making a contribution or subsidy available to provide housing for those who otherwise are condemned to live in sub-standard dwellings.
We must not forget the constructive benefits on the credit side of the ledger. Bad housing is a source of delinquency, bad health, yes, and even crime. In eliminating bad housing, with the assistance of a dominion government subsidy, we are eliminating this costly source of social ills.
I do not need to take up the time of the house in arguing for recognition of the claims of those in the lowest income brackets who ought not to expend more than twenty per cent of their income on housing, because that class and their need have been recognized by the National Housing Act itself. Section 2, subsection 11, recognizes that class of people who ought not to be expending more than twenty per cent of their income on housing,

The Address-Mr. Baker
because if they spend more than that amount they will be doing so at the expense of proper diet and proper clothing.
These citizens in the low income brackets must have more consideration from parliament than the 1944 act will ever give them. That act was largely brought about by the report of the Curtis committee, an eminent committee. Their recommendations were largely adopted by the government with one outstanding exception. That outstanding exception was the provision for subsidizing housing for those in the lowest income brackets. That committee stated:
For the purpose of meeting the low-rental character of the project, i.e., the essential point that its costs cannot be solely met from rental revenues, an annual subsidy is considered the best and most practicable system. It has the merit of being flexible and subject to variation if circumstances or experience demand. It is straightforward in effect, and understandable as a rent reduction fund applied to a clear-cut social welfare purpose. It seems unquestionable that a substantial part of this subsidy should come from the dominion government.
I would conclude with this observation: In this country we have lagged far behind. There is need for an improvement in this legislation, and it must be made. We ought to follow the example of the United Kingdom. They have been subsidizing housing ever since the last war. We are years behind them. We ought to follow the example of the United States which has had a comprehensive measure of this kind since 1937. There are three hundred thousand substandard dwellings occupied in the Dominion of Canada to-day, as found by the Curtis committee. A hundred and twenty-five thousand of these units are in the larger cities, fifty thousand in the smaller cities and a hundred and twenty-five thousand on farms. If parliament and the government do not grapple immediately, courageously and effectively with this problem they will be called to account by the people of Canada. If we grapple with the problem effectively and with determination we shall earn the thanks of a grateful people.

I am a new member in this house. I had not intended to speak so soon in this parliament as I am doing. However, I have heard a lot of remarks made regarding service men. I do not like to use the first person pronoun more often than necessary, but if I do so to-night I ask the house to excuse me. I was overseas and have been in the army for six years. I have fought in two different theatres of war. I was flown back to Canada to contest the election with a fellow member of parliament, the hon. mem-47696-7
ber for Vancou ver-Burrard (Mr. Merritt) across the way, for whom I have the greatest admiration. Everything was very democratic about the whole thing. In the one plane there were four C.C.F., two Liberal and one Progressive Conservative supporter. Of these four C.C.Fs., three were candidates for the federal house and one was for the Ontario provincial house. As we flew over the Atlantic eventually we had to increase our altitude due to cumulus clouds and we reached a height of fifteen thousand feet. At that time, I thought that was the height of democracy.
I have no intention of being acrimonious or bitter in any of my remarks. I am not a politician; I am a soldier; therefore I do not want anybody to take any personal exception to anything that I may say. First of all, I represent the constituency of Shelburne-Yar-mouth-Clare, which is pretty much the extreme east end of Canada and on the Atlantic seaboard. Some of my problems are the same as those of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), particularly fishing. Therefore both ends of Canada have been represented in speeches in this house this afternoon and evening.
The reason I came back to contest the federal election when I was overseas, and it was after V-E day, was just this and simply this, that I had confidence that the government which had carried us victoriously through the European war would be the government which would carry us through to a successful peace.
May I say here, Mr. Speaker, that the British empire has won many wars. That is why we are all here to-night; but something that is even greater than winning wars is the winning of everlasting peace, which has never been done. I maintain that this Liberal government with its trained leaders is the government which can help to take us through to a satisfactory and lasting peace. Possibly some of the hon. members of the opposition are a little too impatient. We did not work up our magnificent navy, army and air force into the fine and efficient fighting machine that it eventually turned out to be in a matter of two weeks. The war has been over for slightly over two weeks. Perhaps we have not admitted that in the house, but that is so, and therefore we have not had very much time in which to convert ourselves from wartime efficiency to peace-time efficiency. But we have these plans made and I maintain that by being patient we worked out our fine fighting machine and that if we shall only have a bit of patience and not draw red herrings across the trail and turn small issues into main issues we shall have a successful

The Address-Mr. Viau

peace and our men will eventually be properly rehabilitated, and that we shall sit at the peace table and make a satisfactory world peace, or at any rate share in it.
Regarding the war memorial in the form of beautifying a larger Ottawa, I am heartily in sympathy with it. There have been hon. members on the opposition side of the house who have been partly in sympathy with it; but they say: "How about wartime housing, and how about various other matters?"
With regard to people who are in distress, I am thoroughly in sympathy with them too, but I believe that both matters can be taken care of, and I believe that the memorial we should have should be a memorial in the capital of Canada, something in which each province of Canada and the territory may feel that they have an equal part and that we shall have a capital of which we shall be proud.
When I was a small boy I visited the city of Washington.' As I walked around that beautiful city I thought to myself it must be wonderful to be an American, and have a capital like that, because I feel that a beautiful capital impresses people from all parts of the country. In the city7 of Edinburgh, Scotland, there is a Little bit of earth from Nova Scotia, the province from which I am pleased to say I come. So I maintain that each province in Canada might well send some of its earth to this city, and that certain parts of the city might be allotted as representing the various provinces.
I believe the principal thing we must realize is that we must get together from coast to coast; the hon. member for Nanaimo and I, as the member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare must get together and work for the general good of Canada. We must not confuse the vast main issues at stake by merely bringing up small, controversial programmes. There is no such thing as a utopia. Though we may try to briDg about that condition, we shall probably never succeed. However, we will do our best and come as close to it as possible. One thing I would, ask hon. members of the opposition is that they have patience. We have not had very long in which to work. This is not the day of the laws of the Medas and Persians. Laws can be changed if it is found that they do not work to the satisfaction of all concerned, and I believe the government which I support will be prepared to make any necessary changes at the proper time.

Mr. Speaker,
before the vote is taken on the motion, perhaps I should say a few words about the government's demobilization policy, particularly in view of the fact that it has been made the subject of criticism in the amendment moved by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken) and in view of the remarks this afternoon of the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. PearkesL
I must confess that, after listening with attention both to the leader of the opposition and to the hon. member for Nanaimo I was unable to ascertain exactly on what grounds they criticized the government's policy. However, that is no doubt due to a defect in my own make-up, rather than to the powers of exposition those hon. members 'possess.
Perhaps, however, it might be well for me to review briefly the 'baas upon which we are proceeding with our policy of demobilizing our armed forces. I am sure hon. members will agree with me that that policy must be fair and that it should be as expeditious and as orderly as possible.
As announced some time ago, the basic principle upon which demobilization is based is that of first-in first-out, the principle that the man with the longest and hardest service , shouild be the first discharged. The hon. member for Nanaimo stated very properly this afternoon that that principle must be subject bo some variation, and that one cannot adopt a hard and fast first-in, first-out rule and expect that the thing will work properly or fairly. The hon. member then proceeded to enumerate -and pretty accurately, I think-those various instances in which we depart from that principle.
The first was on compassionate grounds. As an old professional soldier he knows that that has always been a ground for discharging
The Address-Mr. Abbott

men from the armed services. I take it, therefore, that he does not criticize the government's policy in that particular.
The second ground on which exception, apparently, is made to the basic principle is that where a man has been recommended for early release by the industrial release and selection boards which have been set up under the direction of the Department of Labour, with a view to allowing employers to make application for the early discharge of employees who, they submit, are so-called key men, and for whom it is asked that discharges be granted ahead of their turn. In the cases where recommendation is received from that board the military, naval and, I imagine, the air authorities, will either discharge a man or grant him extended leave. If he is granted extended leave the time during which he engages in civilian occupation prior to his final discharge does not count for gratuity or for rehabilitation grants. The hon. member for Nanaimo did not express his preference one way or the other, as to whether we should abandon that principle. I am sorry he did not say whether we should or not; but I can only assume that, since he did not object to it, he deems it is a proper procedure to follow. That is the second ground upon which a man may be repatriated and discharged, or put on extended leave ahead of his turn.
The third and last ground upon which a man may be returned from overseas other than upon the principle of first-in, first-out is, of course, the obvious one of medical grounds. That is one which has always existed, so far as I know, in all the armed services.
We now come to the men in Canada. As hon. members will appreciate, a week or ten days ago we announced certain extensions to the three points I have mentioned. The first is to allow those who can establish that they have been accepted for admission to a recognized university or educational institution to obtain their discharge ahead of their turn. Again the hon. member for Nanaimo did not indicate whether or not he objected to that procedure. However, I would say to him that, judging by the number of requests I have had from supporters of his party, the great majority of them are in favour of that exception.
The second ground is that a man may be discharged or put upon extended leave ahead of his turn if he is to go to agriculture. Again the hon. member did not object. I have not had a written objection from any hon. member to that procedure. If there is objection I hope hon. members will rise in their places and say that it is wrong. They have not done so yet, and no one has made objection to me as Minister of National Defence.

The third group is the one to which the hon. member referred-and here, may I say, not quite accurately. 1 do not for a moment suggest that he did so purposely. His reference was to the discharging or to the putting of men on extended leave to certain essential occupations.
The situation is this, that in certain occupations designated as essential by the Minister of Labour, including the building industry and the packing house industry, the army will discharge men in Canada, or will release them on extended leave in order to go into those industries. That is policed, if I may use that term, by the ministry of labour. We do not any longer detail any men for civilian work, with the exception of farm labour.
Then there was the final group he mentioned, comprised of men who are discharged as unsuitable for training. That has always been the case so far as I know in every army, and no one should know it better than my hon. friend. He made a plea for reduced taxation, but I do not know whether he feels we should continue at the taxpayers' expense to train unsuitable men in the army. However, if he does I wish he would say so.

speechtext:
As a newly elected member speaking in parliament for the first time I cannot help being impressed when addressing this honourable house. But I know every hon. member is inclined to generosity. I wish first to congratulate you, Mr. Speaker, upon your election to the high office you now occupy. I am sure. you will fulfil your duties with the impartiality and with the dignity you have always shown in your private and public life.
I wish to congratulate the mover (Mr. Benidickson) and the seconder (Mr. Langlois) of the address in reply to the speech from the the throne. Both of these men are young; both of them are heroes; both of them are brilliant speakers. They have proved that war has brought to maturity a new and brilliant generation. Their attitude during the war was a symbol of strength and courage and their attitude before this house is a symbol of determination to win the peace and to assure prosperity for the future of Canada.
(Translation): Mr. Speaker, I did not expect to address this house to-day.
Speakers throughout the country, and especially the hon. member for Nova Scotia and the hon. member for Saskatchewan who preceded me, both of them members of the active army and heroes of this war, did not hesitate, in accordance with their outlook and the purposes they seek to achieve, to uphold the rights of Canadians and to outline the programme they intend to advocate for the welfare of their country.
As representative of a farming community, a constituency which during the war supplied our armed forces with essentials and which also contributed toil, courage and blood, I have deemed it my duty to express to the government of my country my admiration, my esteem and my devotion.
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my remarks I am deeply moved at the thought that I represent to-day the native constituency of a man who was my first counsellor, the idol of his province, who has symbolized the spirit of Canada in its purest and finest form, the late hon. Ernest Lapointe. He was among the first to add lustre to the name of Kamouraska and it was he who courageously and proudly wore the political mantle of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, the great Canadian leader whose memory still endures.
I stated a moment ago that the constituency of Kamouraska is an essentially agricultural community. It is composed of parishes where farming is the chief industry and lumbering comes next in importance.
As several are aware, there is in my constituency a classical college of foremost importance, where great men have received their education, and I would be afraid to offend the modesty of several members of this house if I were to single out those who attended Ste. Anne college.
In addition there is a high school of agriculture and fishing.
Agriculture, especially during the period of reconstruction which is now beginning, must enlist the assistance of science and resort to the most modern practices.
We have experts, as well as distinguished and experienced agronomists, we have specialized courses through which numerous technicians have received their training, and who come not only from the district of Kamouraska but also from the region of Quebec city where they have assisted in the agricultural development through their talents, their culture and their scientific knowledge they have won recognition throughout the country.
The Address-Mr. Marquis

May I add, Mr. Speaker, that there is also in my constituency a Dominion experimental station which enables us to engage in practical studies and scientific research in agriculture and constitutes a perfect organization for the prosperity not only of the locality but of the whole province of Quebec.
In the recent election, like most of those who sit here, I was privileged to have opponents. One of them had been a Conservative ever since his early childhood and perhaps since his birth. Probably on account of some political reactions which exist in certain quarters, he suddenly felt an urge of independence which led him to a crushing defeat. The other one was an advocate of Social Credit; he was quite modest and preached a theory which did not succeed in rallying enough believers to save his deposit.
The people of the constituency of Kamou-raska, who are peaceful, honest and hardworking citizens, believed in their country, in their leader, and they gave their full confidence to the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mackenzie King). It is a testimonial much greater than the one I could give myself. The preachings of extremists, the criticism of independents, the new theories of every kind could not sway the confidence of sincere and loyal people who remembered that in our country there is a man who, especially since 1935, when he fell heir to the sorry legacy of unemployment, set about his work, fought and carried out social policies in order to place this country on a basis of progress. At the time when the country was being stabilized, war broke out, a war that threatened not only Canada but the whole world.
We have heard this truth proclaimed in this house, on various tones, it is true, but all agreed that Canada was in danger, that our freedoms were jeopardized, that the survival of Christianity itself was at stake. The people of my constituency, together with most of Canada's citizens, understood that one man, in spite of the heavy burden he had carried in the past, managed to avoid all pitfalls, to overcome all obstacles and to lead us through the whole war to ultimate victory. This man is the Prime Minister of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, I know I am expressing the views of my constituents when I say that we are grateful to the Prime Minister for the way he has warded off all dangers and we thank divine providence that he is still in our midst.
There are speakers in this house who, a few months ago, asked for total mobilization of our man-power and who now want the army demobilized even before the war is officially ended. Yet, the programme of the administra-r\Tr. Marquis. 1
tion in this regard clearly provides for as prompt a return of our men as most of our service men themselves would wish. It is a wonder to me that those w'ho purport to vindicate the rights of our soldiers who fought on the various battlefields, should preach a doctrine which is not adhered to by our military men. Never, in a speech from the throne, has there been outlined so comprehensive a programme providing every possible means of reorganization and reconstruction in Canada. Does any one claim that the speech from the throne should specify the exact amounts that should be appropriated for each particular measure? I do not think any member of this house would entertain such an idea. But this programme enables all persons of good will to cooperate in the development of the country, and to contribute to veterans' assistance. This policy promotes the agricultural production, to assist famished peoples. It is the government of our country who offer a helping hand to the poor, the famished and the unfortunate.
Who are those who oppose the government measures? Who are those who fight the adoption of this policy intended to help the peoples of the overseas countries to get sufficient clothing, food and fuel? They are the gentlemen of the opposition, sitting on your left, near you, Mr. Speaker.
At the close of a conflict which has jeopardized not only our freedom of speech and our wealth, but even what I would call our right to live, our right to leave an inheritance, however small, to posterity, we should all unite in close cooperation in order to attain to a spirit truly, fully and solely Canadian in character.
I have never concurred in the opinions of any extremist. They are sowers of disunity, whatever province they hail from. I am more convinced than ever that, in this house, we all aim, now more than ever, at unity and harmony.
Mr. Speaker, while reading magazines, periodicals, newspapers I have often noted with regret the tone adopted by some speechi-fiers and even the ideas they dared to express. May we now say that such incidents are but the exception and that in our beloved Canada, the representatives of the people, maintaining their personal identity, remaining faithful to their race and beliefs and respecting other creeds and races, may we now say, Mr. Speaker, that all of us shall rally as Canadians around a symbol, a national flag which will serve as guide to every one?

The Address-Mr. Merritt
Mr. Speaker, I know of no one in this house or even in the country who does not wish for real unity in Canada. I express the solemn hope that before long, Canada will have a recognized national anthem which all her citizens to sing before a flag around which we will gather.
Some members of the house object to the government's policy. Do they oppose the San Francisco charter, a pact which represents the resultant of the discussions held by the United Nations? Does not the speech from the throne reflect the spirit not only of Canada but of the whole civilized world toward postwar reconstruction when it asks to approve the San Francisco charter? Do these honourable gentlemen oppose the adoption of the address in reply to the speech from the throne because the Canadian government intends to proceed as rapidly as possible with the conversion of war industries into peace-time industries? As some would say, Mr. Speaker, if those gentlemen were in the place of the government, would the reconversion of those industries come more rapidly or perhaps as quickly as some among them transformed themselves into independents in the province of Quebec. Those honourable gentlemen governed this country before 1935, and to my knowledge there were no miracles in political administration during this five-year plan. There were indeed, Mr. Speaker, timely suggestions from some members who sit to your left, and I know that all the members of the government are ready to consider suggestions that may be accepted and adapted to the political conditions as they new exist in this country. I listened with much attention to the leader of the C.C.F. party (Mr. Coldwell), who, besides having remarkable parliamentary qualifications, certainly made, in his speech, a few suggestions which may, at a later time, affect this country's policies. I know that the Prime Minister has long since always carefully considered the opinions expressed by the various groups. Besides, those who are quite earnest in their criticism realize that the leaders in the administration cannot always adapt all the suggestions made to existing conditions. Evolution is inherent to politics just as it is to life; and, in the field of soldiers' reestablishment, or of reconversion of war industries to peacetime enterprises, those who urge, for the time being, a fixed and definite plan, and for years to come, a scaled plan, forget that the future is veiled to us, that we cannot know in advance what circumstance the country will face in a few months or perhaps a few weeks. That is what the government must keep in mind while carrying out its policy.
Mr. Speaker, I trust that the government which directed our war effort, maintained peace at home and rallied all Canadian forces to fight the enemy, once again, I trust that this government is qualified to effect civilian reestablishment, to help in the country's reconstruction and finally to grant our working classes the stability and safeguards they expect. The government which allayed the dangers of inflation will prevent deflation. The administration which, during the war, checked capitalistic abuses will not allow capitalism to stand in the way of a proper and just redistribution of the wealth of our country; that is why it has granted family allowances which will allow children to prepare for the future, to be properly clothed and fed, to receive a better education. In fact, the Liberal administration did not wait until the close of the war. At the most tragic periods, when Canadian lives were being lost in battle, our government turned its attention to our manpower and the protection of childhood; it decided to protect the working classes, the little people to ensure that, in our country, the middle class would be immune from capitalistic abuses. That is what the Liberal government has done for the good of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, in concluding my remarks I apologize to the hon. members of this house as it is the first time that I have had an opportunity to address them. I admit that I gained my inspiration in the study of Canadian politics, in my love of country, in my admiration and esteem for my leaders, in my faith in their sound policies. I admire their moderation and the efforts which they are making to ensure Canadian unity.
(Text): In conclusion, I thank God for having given Canada our Prime Minister, and for having given him the necessary health and strength to preside over the destinies of the nation during the war and during peacetime.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to apologize to the house for intervening in this debate at such a late hour, but I find it necessary to do so for definite reasons. You will excuse a new member for having perhaps misunderstood the purpose of this debate, which is on the address in reply to the speech from the throne, the amendment thereto and the subamendment offered by the group to my left. It does not seem to me that the purpose of this debate is fully served simply by rushing to a vote on the question without having canvassed it properly. And this is what I mean by canvassing it properly. It was my understanding that in this debate there would be an opportunity for the ministers of the crown
The Address-Mr. Merritt

to make to this country public statements which they have failed to make all summer on the great and important matters which have been exercising our people during the past few months, whether or not the members of the government know it. Before this debate terminates I hope we may hear not from private members on the government side, replying to the amendment offered by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Bracken), but from the responsible ministers of the crown charged with the duty of seeing to it that we have jobs and housing, and that our men overseas get a proper deal when they return to this country. It is these hon. gentlemen whom I feel the country wishes to hear from in this debate.
I was very glad when Minister of National Defence (Mr. Abbott) rose to speak to the amendment in regard to the service personnel overseas and to answer the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes), who made such a telling speech this afternoon. Let me say to the minister at once that I know he was not responsible for the situation in which the government now finds itself in reference to the army. That situation sprang from the evil seed of the man-power policy which has been wrong from the beginning, and the minister has no responsibility for that. When he spoke to-night I thought I was going to hear what the country wants to hear; but all I heard from the minister was a deprecatory statement in reference to the speech of the hon. member for Nanaimo. The minister spoke of all the various ways in which men get out of the army now, as though the hon. member for Nanaimo was complaining, and as though this amendment complained, in regard to specific minor details. The hon. member for Nanaimo read out that list only to show the house the wide variety of methods by which people can get out of the army to-day, ranging from compassionate leave, which may be a perfectly good ground, down to "unlikely to become an efficient soldier," or "not amenable to discipline" which I say here is a perfectly bad ground.

speechtext: Is this the courtesy extended to an hon. member in his first speech in the house?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I thank my hon. friend, but I need no such courtesies; I will answer any question that is asked. I will leave that question to the judgment of the house and the country, and speak now to the other two parts of the amendment. At least we can say that the Minister of National Defence rose in his place. What of the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe), who is responsible, I take it, for jobs and housing? Has he risen in his place during this debate? Not at all; we have not heard from him. The country wishes to hear from him during this debate. Lest he should be under any misapprehension as to the nature of this amendment, I say to this house that the amendment expresses exactly the feeling of this country against the government to-day. The country is both anxious and critical. The war is over, and the country is anxious about the ability of this government to show the way to full employment. The country is critical in regard to the lack of leadership exhibited by this government at the inception of the reconstruction period.

speechtext:
I hear hon. gentlemen
opposite laugh. I say to them that for a long time they have claimed to be the leaders of this country. I say to them now that this country has been carrying the government on its back for a long time. Hon. members opposite may be thankful that this is a great country, and that as such it is capable of carrying even hon. members opposite on its back.
I should like to make another point about the amendment, lest it be thought that it should be allowed to go by default-like jobs

The Address-Mr. Merritt
and housing. The amendment is a criticism striking directly at the capacity of hon. members who form the government to lead the people of the country. I wish to say right now that, unlike my hon. friends to my left, who believe that w*e need a new social order, I have believed for many years-and there are a great number of people who agree with me, and who will always agree with me-that we need no new social order in order to have full employment in our country.
What we do need, and what we have not had in my adult life-and what I fear we can never have from this government-is "action" to give us full employment. The people of Canada are a reasonable people. I do not believe they expect very much, perhaps not as much as they have a right to expect, from the government of their country. I do not think that they call for utopia, or even that they mind being inconvenienced by lack of housing, or being laid off from jobs during a difficult period.
But what they do mind, what exasperates them and prompts them to talk among themselves, as they are talking across the country to-day, is complete inaction on the part of the government to face up to problems which, although they may not be of great concern to the government, concern the people deeply. If the government has no action to offer, as I suspect it has not, then the people might be satisfied if an explanation were offered to them, and I am suggesting that such explanation should be made in this debate, and that the matter ought not to go by default. The government should explain when people might expect to find those jobs, and when they might expect to see those houses.
When the amendment was offered by the leader of the opposition the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) sought to turn it off by expressing his satisfaction in the results of the general election held in June. The hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth-Clare (Mr. Baker), for whom I have very great respect indeed, and with whom I did not expect to take issue so early in the debate, talked about these matters of housing and jobs as if they were only small issues.
I wish to dispel any impression the Prime Minister may have sought to create to the effect that he is protected by the mandate he received from the people on June 11. I should like to recount a little history-even at this late hour-and it will not be ancient history. The history I shall offer will be very modern in the history of Canada, and although it is confined to the city of Vancouver, one of the 47696-8
constituencies of which I have the honour to represent, I am sure it is applicable throughout Canada.
Apparently some hon. members do not realize just what the situation is in Canada with respect to housing and jobs. So that they may do so, let me go on with my history. In May came V-E day, and in June the general election. I am not going to go at all into the history before the election; so that that excuse is not available to hon. members opposite. The people of Canada did not mind being badly housed before V-E day, because they had a war to fight. They did not even mind being badly housed after V-E day because there was still a war to fight. But they did expect-indeed, they have been promised by this government-that there would be action in respect of housing at once.
In the city of Vancouver there has been no action, and I shall recount to the house just what the situation is there. It now has in its population about 60,000 extra souls over its pre-war population. May I point out, in passing, that forty-eight per cent of the male population of service age in British Columbia volunteered for the armed forces. Those men are returning in ever-increasing numbers.
I have heard the over-all shortage of houses in Vancouver estimated as high as 20,000, but in my presentation this evening I shall settle :or a very much smaller number than that. Let us, for the sake of this discussion, say that the number is only 5,000 or 10,000. On a certain day in August there were 1,400 veterans of this war who had served overseas, whose names were recorded on the books of the emergency shelter administration as having been placed in housing so unsuitable that even that harassed authority thought it should try again, if it could, to get better accommodation for them.
Let me place before the house two illustrations of how those men are living. In the first place, they are living in basements and attics. In the second place, they are living in that new and great Canadian national institution, the chicken-house duplex. And when I say that I am not attempting to crack a joke, but rather, have reference to veterans living in chicken-houses.
Let me give another illustration, from another point of view. There was one case of twenty-five men, women and children who were sharing one bathroom. If hon. members will reflect for a while on that situation they will readily realize the inconvenience entailed.
I ask the house this question: Of what use to the country and to the veterans is a veterans charter? Of what use to them is a

The Address-Mr. Merritt
welcome home and a civic reception, if, when they reach their homes, they must live under conditions such as I have described? What we want from the government is not grandiose plans, white papers and legislation. By offering us those they perform only half their job. We must have executive action to translate those plans into benefits placed in the hands of the men, women and children of this country.
That is all that will satisfy the people of Canada, and it is not too much to ask from the ministers concerned. Let me deal in further detail with the subject of housing. I have said that people might not mind living in chicken-houses, or might not complain about it. But what has the government done? Despite the promises made, the only housing activity of which I know in Vancouver this past summer was an application, by advertisement, for the registration of construction workers, and the throwing of Wartime Housing Limited into the already too small market for supplies.
At the moment the difficulty with the housing situation is not that of low rental housing, or of any social aspect of the question. It is simply a question of shortage of supply. That is certainly the case in Vancouver. So far as I am aware there is no authority in this country which has the job of getting after the bottlenecks in supplies. I made a little pilgrimage in Vancouver just to find out what the situation might be in this respect. I visited the wartime prices and trade board; the controller of construction; the emergency shelter administration; the mayor of the city; the private contractors' association; and I visited other agencies around town. Every one was most helpful, particularly the civil servants. They were all working desperately to try to get around this shortage, but none of them had any power to do a thing, none of them had any full responsibility. I could not find a man in Vancouver who had authority, responsibility or full knowledge about the housing shortage. That is what is at the bottom of this shortage, and nothing else. There has been no action in getting after the bottlenecks and trying to get rid of them.
I go on with my history and I mention what happened in July. In July we had a large and important strike at the American Can Company in Vancouver which supplies all the cans for western Canada. The strike lasted for fourteen days, and by the end of that time almost all the primary producers who tinned their products were desperate because their goods were spoiling. They were losing money day after day. The strike [Mr. Merritt.)
was on that old familiar issue, the closed shop. Did the government take any action? Yes, after two weeks-just in the nick of time-and, after all the agony had been gone through by the people on the Pacific coast because of the fear that their merchandise would spoil; after all the loss they had suffered through having to shut off production-the government acted and called in someone to take over the plant and to arrange a compromise. Why could they not have acted first? Why could they not have taken over the plant as soon as the strike occurred and then adjudicated and thus saved from loss the consumers and producers of primary products who had no concern with the strike? How many times and in how many places are we to have strikes on this old familiar issue without government action?
I come now to August, to V-J day. They rang the air raid siren in Vancouver to signalize V-J day. I wondered why and I soon found out. There had been some small celebration, a natural blowing off of steam which did not last too long. We then noticed an ominous undercurrent of wonder and a little bit of fear on the part of some people that there were to be no jobs in the shipyards or in the aircraft factories. The workers in these factories in Vancouver have done a magnificent job in this war and they now amount to a considerable number.
I tell you what happened, and it came very soon too. Private notices were sent out by these companies laying off the workers. There was no word whatever from Ottawa as to what was to happen to the workers; they were simply laid off by means of a notice from the private companies. The government just ignored the fact that this was going to raise a serious situation immediately. I do not suggest that the Minister of Reconstruction (Mr. Howe) should have provided each of these men with a job. Under our system these men will find new jobs, but I do suggest that the minister should have laid some plans so that, even if V-J day took him slightly by surprise, he would have been able to make a public statement and give reassurance to the workers in Vancouver and other parts of the country. Perhaps he could have told them that he had been taken slightly by surprise, but to "hold on" because in a certain length of time the plans he had made to bring these plants back into production under other circumstances would bear fruit and jobs would be available. He could have said that in the meantime his advice was such and so. But there was no action; there was not even a statement of reassurance. I may say to the

The Address-Mr. Merritt
house that out there on the Pacific coast we notice that lack of advice from the fountain of all authority in the country. We would be interested in having a little bit of attention paid to our problems.
The public is looking for reassurance. It is looking for leadership at once in this postwar reconstruction period. The record of this government since the general election in providing leadership for the people of this country is a sorry one indeed. I would not say that the people of Vancouver are down about it at all. I do not think they expected very much more. They have maintained their spirit, but they and the people of Canada are high-spirited. They are exasperated; that is the only word for it. They do not want anything too wonderful; they want action, that is all.
I should like to point out one way in which the inaction and lack of leadership from this government has affected things out in that part of the country from which I come. The housing crisis and the job crisis have caused many public statements to be made at many public meetings. The mayor of the city and the provincial government have been badgered by organization after organization to do work that this government ought to be doing. I say to hon. gentlemen opposite that it is not fair that provincial and municipal governments should be badgered, and perhaps lose the confidence of the people, when they have not the power to act before this government has given them a lead. The situation is quite serious and I am sure it will bring unwise political repercussions out there.
What I want and what I say the country wants is action and leadership. And for this reason. I say to the house that laissez-faire is dead. I know the house will agree with me, but let us consider for a moment just what that means. In short, it means this. When the people of Canada gave the present government of this country a mandate on June 11 to form a government, they did not elect them negatively to maintain free enterprise in being as the economic system of this country. They gave them a mandate positively to get in there and to make free enterprise work to produce satisfactory conditions for all Canadians. I want to say to the government that they have made a bad start because what is wanted in order to make free enterprise work is leadership. Leadership in reforming and controlling private enterprise when it does not serve the interests of the public, but, above all, what is wanted is leadership which promotes public confidence in our joint ability to perform the great task ahead. I say to hon. gentlemen opposite that if they 47696-8J
have not that confidence or if they make the people of Canada doubt their joint ability for the tasks ahead, as has been done this summer, this government will not succeed in carrying out what the people of Canada want them to do. If we have not confidence in our ability to create full employment, then all fails.
The end of laissez-faire means another thing. It means that the government are no longer solely the administrators of the affairs of this country; that they can be content just to let things go. The government are ultimately responsible for every part of our national life, and there is no ill which befalls the people of this country which it is not the duty of the government to correct. If they are to correct all those ills, they must get a new outlook. They must give us that leadership and action which I have emphasized to-night. With that in mind I wish in the few minutes remaining to me to offer two concrete suggestions on leadership, and I ask all hon. members who have served in the armed forces to see if they do not go all the way with me.
First of all, I say that the time has passed when ministers of the crown can remain in Ottawa and property conduct the affairs of this country from the capital. The ministers must get out and get around the country, and they can do it now by aeroplane, which is very fortunate, now that we have come to the end of laissez-faire. They must get around the country to find out what the people want and to see how their legislation is working and whether or not the benefits are getting to the people. I liken a minister of the crown and his deputy minister to a general and his chief staff officer. All hon. members who have served in either war will go with me when I say that a general is not a good general if he is not out seeing his troops. After a general has made his decision and given his orders to his chief staff officer, he gets out on the ground and sees how that order is working out, and by personal reconnaissance he gathers the information that enables him to make his next decision. Such a course must be followed by ministers of the crown if they are to lead the people of this country successfully.

speechtext: Sounds like regimentation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: It is not; it is leadership, but the hon. member would not know the difference. My time is almost up.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Go ahead.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
The next thing the government must do is to take the people into its confidence. You can never lead them, if I. may
The Address-Mr. Merritt

say so to hon. gentlemen, without telling them what you are going to do and how you are going to do it.
Another thing that one can learn in the armed forces, and even when one is not in the armed forces-but very few people, including myself, do-is the vital importance of time. I say to the ministers of the crown that they must take the public into their confidence-not only in routine press conferences which serve their purposes very well; but also by special press conferences and by specially timed appeals over the broadcasting system and by specially timed visits throughout the country, as these emergencies come up, instead of doing as they have done this summer, just letting things go by default. If you tell the people of this country what you want them to do, they will do it for you. They have proved that veiy well in the last six years. I never saw any troops, and I do not know of any people, who will do anything that you want them to do if you do not first tell them what it is that you want them to do.
If I had time I could make other suggestions as to how hon. gentlemen opposite could give leadership to this country. The suggestions I have made so far are not, of course, exhaustive, and if the ministers of the crown wish to give leadership to the people of this country they can easily find many additional ways of doing it. I would not have the temerity to tell them how to do their jobs. That would ill become a new member and a young man. I know they are able administrators.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speechtext:
Surely hon. gentlemen do not take too much pleasure in that remark. Surely they must be good administrators in order to sit in the high places they occupy; they must have something to their credit. I know they are good administrators, but I say that in this new era after the war they must be more than administrators-they have to be leaders. I want them to carry this message away with them, and I believe I speak for a very large part of the people of Canada when I say this. The government must have a new approach to present-day problems, and if I may say this without being offensive, but simply to make my point, I would say that what the government need is what we needed in the army, a sort of mental "battle drill" for cabinet ministers.
But to come back to the most important point, let the government make a start at giving this leadership that is needed. Let us have from the Minister of Reconstruction and Supply a statement on how Canadians may expect to get jobs in the immediate future. Let

the government tell us what they are going to do about these questions such as severance pay that are vexing labour. Let the government tell us how soon we may expect a housing expediter and how soon action will be taken to loosen bottlenecks in supplies in order that houses may be built throughout Canada.
On motion of Mr. Ross (Souris) the debate was adjourned.
